opus-5.5.text:
Well, I've always believed that you really can't separate the two. Going back to my early work on chip multiprocessors, the lesson was that hardware innovation only matters if software can actually exploit it. So with Step, Streaming Tensor Programs, we started from the software side and asked: what is the right abstraction for expressing the computations people care about today, things like large language models, mixture-of-experts, attention with dynamic shapes, and how do we map that efficiently onto dataflow hardware?

The key insight is that modern ML workloads are increasingly dynamic. You have data-dependent control flow, variable sequence lengths, routing decisions in mixture-of-experts layers that you don't know until runtime. Traditional static dataflow abstractions struggle with that, because they assume you can plan everything ahead of time. Step gives you a streaming abstraction where tensors flow as streams of tiles through a graph of operators, and it has explicit constructs for dynamism, so you can express things like dynamic tiling or dynamic routing directly in the program.

What makes this a hardware-software co-design story is that the abstraction is designed with the hardware in mind. It exposes the things that actually determine performance on a spatial dataflow accelerator: memory hierarchy, on-chip buffering, bandwidth, how much parallelism you allocate to each operator. So the programmer, or a compiler, can reason about those trade-offs at a high level and get performance estimates without having to go all the way down to RTL. That lets us explore the design space much faster: you can ask what happens if I change the tile size, or add more on-chip memory, or rebalance the pipeline, and get meaningful answers quickly.

And it flows the other direction too. When we see what kinds of programs people want to write in Step, that tells us what the next generation of hardware should support efficiently. That's really the philosophy we've followed with Plasticine and then at SambaNova: you design the programming model and the architecture together, so neither one is an afterthought. If you only optimize the hardware, you end up with a chip that's hard to program. If you only optimize the software, you're leaving a lot of efficiency on the table. The interesting research lives at that interface.

r001.rationale: The response says Step started from the software side, but does not state that the research is further along on software than on hardware implementation.

r002.rationale: The response discusses designing the programming model and architecture together, but does not say the researchers have not disclosed a hardware implementation because its details remain undetermined.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. For me, the relationship between software and hardware is really the whole story. The way I think about it is that you have to co-design them, because if you design the hardware first and then try to bolt the software on afterward, you end up with something that's either very hard to program or very inefficient, and usually both.

So with Streaming Tensor Programs, or STeP, the starting point was actually a question about abstraction. If you look at the dominant abstraction today, it's the GPU model. It's a bulk synchronous model, you launch a kernel, it does some work, it writes results back to memory, you launch the next kernel. That maps well to the kind of dense matrix multiplication that dominated early deep learning. But as models have gotten more complicated, with things like mixture of experts, dynamic sparsity, attention with variable sequence lengths, and the whole decoding process in large language models, that bulk synchronous model starts to break down. You spend a lot of time moving data back and forth through the memory hierarchy, and a lot of effort writing custom kernels and fusing things by hand just to get reasonable efficiency.

So the idea with STeP was to ask, what if the programming model were fundamentally about streams of tensors flowing through a dataflow graph, where operations are pipelined and the data never has to go back to memory between stages unless it actually needs to? Once you commit to that abstraction, it tells you something about what the hardware should look like. It wants to be a spatial, dataflow architecture, something like the reconfigurable dataflow machines we've been working on with SambaNova, where you have a fabric of compute units and memory units and you map the graph onto it so that intermediate results stay on chip.

But it also works in the other direction. Having built that kind of hardware, we learned what the hardware is actually good at and what's awkward for it, and that fed back into the abstraction. For example, dynamic behavior, like data-dependent control flow or variable-sized tensors, is something you have to think very carefully about in a streaming model, because you can't just assume everything is statically shaped. So a lot of the research effort went into making the programming model expressive enough to capture those dynamic patterns while still being something a compiler can map efficiently onto a spatial architecture.

The thing I keep coming back to is that the abstraction layer is where the leverage is. If you get the abstraction right, then the compiler can do the hard work of scheduling and placement, the hardware can be specialized without becoming unprogrammable, and the people writing models don't have to think about any of it. If you get it wrong, every new model architecture turns into a hand-optimization project. So in our group, hardware and software people really sit in the same room, and the design of the one is constantly informed by the constraints and opportunities of the other.

r001.rationale: The response describes software and hardware as co-designed and says the team has built relevant hardware, but it does not say the research is further along on the software side.

r002.rationale: The response discusses a spatial dataflow architecture and implementation challenges, but does not say the researchers have withheld implementation details because they have not yet determined how the hardware implementation will work.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as a co-design problem. You don’t want to design the hardware in isolation and then ask the software people to figure out how to use it. You want to start with the computation you’re trying to express, understand where the parallelism is and how the data moves, and develop the software abstraction and the hardware together.

With Step Streaming Tensor Programs, the idea is to give the compiler enough information about the structure of the computation that it can map that computation efficiently onto the hardware. Streaming lets you think about data flowing between operations, rather than every operation having to write its results back to memory before the next one can begin.

So there’s a feedback loop. The programming model tells us what capabilities the hardware needs, and the hardware tells us which aspects of the computation the compiler needs to expose and manage. The goal is to get efficiency without making the programmer handle every hardware detail.

r001.rationale: The response describes software and hardware being developed together, but does not say the research is further along on the software side.

r002.rationale: The response gives no statement that implementation details have not been disclosed because the hardware implementation is not yet precisely determined.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of software and hardware as things you have to develop together. The software tells you what computation you want to perform, and the hardware determines how efficiently you can carry it out. If you design either one in isolation, you can miss opportunities that only become apparent when you look across that boundary.

With Step Streaming Tensor Programs, the idea is to have a way of expressing computation that makes that relationship explicit. We want the compiler to see how data moves through the computation and exploit the parallelism available in the hardware. And, in the other direction, what we learn from mapping those programs should inform the architecture. So it’s an iterative process: the programming model, the compiler, and the hardware evolve together.

r001.rationale: The response says software, compiler, and hardware evolve together, but does not state that the research is further along on the software side.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that the researchers have not disclosed a hardware implementation or that they have not yet determined precisely how it will work.
